title: Breathing in pain
hookLine: a Tibetan Buddhist practice: breathe in others' pain, breathe out relief, gently and never forced
carry: in with pain, out with relief

lines: BREATHE IN CALM, BREATHE OUT STRESS?
cards: Breathe in calm, breathe out stress. That's the usual instruction in a breathing exercise. A practice from Tibetan Buddhism turns it around on purpose.
Breathe in someone's pain. Breathe out relief, toward them. It sounds backwards.
It even sounds a little risky, like inviting a cold into the house. And yet Tibetan teachers have taught it for a long time as a way to grow compassion.
Its name is today's word, and how the teachers handle it matters as much as the practice itself.

teach.b: First, the name. Tonglen is Tibetan for sending and taking. On the in-breath you take in the suffering of someone, and on the out-breath you send them whatever relief you'd wish for them: warmth, ease, rest.
Tonglen belongs to a Tibetan Buddhist training called lojong, which means mind training.
Tradition traces it to the Indian teacher Atisha, and later teachers gathered it into short slogans meant to be carried through an ordinary day.
One of them, in plain paraphrase, says to practice sending and taking in turn, riding them on the breath. Third, why it runs this way. A mind tends to pull away from pain and reach for comfort.

teach.h: IT REVERSES THE HABIT OF PULLING AWAY.
teach.b: Tonglen reverses that habit on purpose, as a way of opening the heart instead of closing it. Teachers present it as a training in compassion, not as magic that moves someone's illness into your body.

teach.h: IN WITH PAIN, OUT WITH RELIEF.
teach.b: Pema Chödrön, a modern teacher in this lineage, suggests starting close: with your own pain, or with one person you love, before anyone harder. And the practice widens from there: whoever else is hurting the same way.
Two words carry the whole method: never forced. Tonglen isn't a test of how much pain a person can swallow. It's a few honest breaths in the direction of someone else.

how: Tibetan Buddhists practice tonglen as part of lojong, or mind training, breathing in suffering and breathing out relief; teachers suggest beginning with their own pain or a loved one.

games.q: you've begun tonglen for a friend in pain. on the third in-breath it starts to feel like too much. what now?
o: push through and take in more.
come back to your own breath, gently.
switch to someone you can't stand.
games.why: the practice is gentle and never forced. coming back to your own breath is part of it, and teachers like Pema Chödrön start close for exactly this reason.

practice: Bring to mind one person you care about who's struggling.
For three breaths, breathe in a little of their heaviness, like warm, dark air, only as much as feels okay, and breathe out ease toward them, like cool, clear light; then simply breathe.
If it feels like too much, come back to your own breath, which is part of the practice too, and if you pray, you can hold their name.
